title: ARINBEV: Bird's-Eye View Layout Estimation with Autoregressive Modeling
one_liner: The paper uses a one-step-at-a-time decoder to build bird's-eye view maps by capturing how traffic elements depend on each other.
lead: Autonomous vehicles need to understand road layouts from camera images. Older methods treat each road element separately, but in reality roads follow strict rules: lanes curve together, stop lines come before crosswalks, crosswalks align with sidewalks. ARINBEV builds maps one element at a time, keeping track of how earlier choices constrain later ones, making maps that follow real road logic.

problem.h2: Road maps that ignore how pieces connect
paras: Autonomous vehicles need to know where roads, lanes, and pedestrian paths are. They look at camera images and build a bird's-eye view map: a top-down picture labeling each pixel as drivable area, lane, crosswalk, or something else.

Older methods treat each label as independent. They ask: for this pixel, is it a lane? For that pixel, is it a crosswalk? This ignores a key fact: roads are built by engineers following strict rules. Stop lines must come before crosswalks. Lane dividers follow road curves. Sidewalks align with crosswalks. When a method ignores these dependencies, it produces maps with nonsense: lanes that double back, crosswalks floating in midair, or dividers that do not match the road shape.

callout.html: Maps built pixel-by-pixel ignore how traffic elements must relate to each other, leading to geometrically invalid and unsafe predictions.

steps.text: Take the front-facing camera view and encode it into numerical features.
Begin building the top-down map by placing the first road element.
Given what has been placed so far, predict the next element's location and type.
Add each new element one at a time, always using earlier placements to decide.
Continue until all road elements are positioned and labeled.

paras: The key change is how the model generates the map. Instead of deciding all pixels at once (in parallel), it predicts them sequentially: one road element after another. Each prediction sees all the earlier choices, so it can enforce consistency.

hidden.h2: Semantic consistency: enforcing valid road logic
hidden.name: semantic consistency across elements
paras: The hidden quantity the paper measures is semantic consistency: whether the generated map respects the structural relationships that real roads must follow. For example, a stop line should appear before (upstream of) the crosswalk it guards; lane dividers should curve smoothly and not intersect the drivable area they bound.

ARINBEV enforces this by predicting elements in an order that respects dependencies. When the model places a crosswalk, it has already placed the approach lane and stop line. This means the decoder can learn that crosswalks only appear in certain configurations, and it can refuse placements that violate road logic. The paper measures this indirectly through map accuracy on real road datasets.

heat.caption: Darker means more constrained by earlier elements. Marked elements must appear in order.

reads.html: Before placing a crosswalk, the decoder has already decided where lanes and approach lanes are, so it only places crosswalks where they geometrically fit.
The step-by-step (autoregressive) approach breaks down the map into a sequence of predictions, where each element's likelihood depends on the positions and types of all previously placed elements.

mechanism.h2: Why sequential generation enforces road structure
paras: The mechanism is constraint propagation through ordering. When you predict one road element at a time, each new element sees all the prior decisions. This means invalid configurations become unlikely: if a lane is already drawn, the model learns never to place a crosswalk on top of it, because during training it always saw correct examples where that does not happen. The decoder gradually builds up context about the road's shape and how pieces fit together.

In contrast, a method that predicts all pixels in parallel has no way to enforce consistency. Each pixel is scored independently, and later you get nonsense. With sequential prediction, each step is shaped by what came before: the decoder cannot place a stop line where the road curves sharply because the model learned from real data that stop lines are perpendicular to lane flow.

The single-stage decoder-only design avoids the complexity of multi-stage training or separate components that must be aligned. Instead, one transformer (or similar) reads the camera features and outputs elements one at a time, using its own earlier outputs as context. This simplifies training and shrinks the number of weights that need to be stored and trained.

stages.s: Decoder reads image and prior elements
Predict next element type and location

math.h2: The probability of a complete map
math.words: The total probability of the map is the product of probabilities for each element, where each element's probability is conditioned on all prior elements.
symbols: probability that the generated map is correct
the type and location of road element i
probability of element i given all prior elements
total number of elements in the map

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a road has 3 elements: lane, stop line, crosswalk.
Prior training: when lane is placed, stop line follows 90% of the time. P(stop line | lane) = 0.90.
When both lane and stop line are in place, crosswalk appears 85% of the time. P(crosswalk | lane, stop line) = 0.85.
Full map probability: P(lane) * P(stop line | lane) * P(crosswalk | lane, stop line) = 0.5 * 0.90 * 0.85 = 0.38.
A broken sequence (lane, crosswalk, stop line) would give: 0.5 * 0.05 * 0.10 = 0.0025 — much lower, so the model avoids it.

math.note: The math factorizes the map into a causal chain where each element's likelihood depends on the prior structure, making the decoder learn which configurations are geometrically valid.

charts.title: Older models (multi-stage encoder-decoder)
charts.note: Good accuracy but slow to train and memory-heavy because they separate the image-reading part from the map-building part, and both parts must be trained together.

charts.title: ARINBEV (single-stage autoregressive)
charts.note: Higher accuracy and faster training because the single decoder that reads images AND outputs elements can be trained end-to-end without aligning two separate components. Fewer parts means fewer weights to store and train.

items.html: If the model learns the wrong element ordering, the conditioning will enforce the wrong constraints. For example, if the model learns to place crosswalks before stop lines, it will never learn that stop lines come first, and maps will be consistently wrong.
If the first element is placed incorrectly (e.g., a lane offset to the side), all subsequent elements will be positioned relative to that wrong lane. The error propagates forward.
If the training data has few examples of unusual road layouts (e.g., a complex interchange), the model learns the common patterns well but fails on rare cases.
The model learns an ordering that matches real road construction logic (which is deterministic). The decoder then uses the prior elements' positions to place each new element consistently.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy autonomous driving scene with a simple road (one lane, one stop line, one crosswalk). Give the decoder a camera image from that scene. Have it generate the bird's-eye map autoregressively and check three things: (1) Does it place elements in the correct order (lane before stop line before crosswalk)? (2) Does the geometric configuration respect road rules (stop line is perpendicular to lane; crosswalk is perpendicular to stop line)? (3) If you perturb the camera image (add noise or change the viewpoint slightly), does the map degrade gracefully or does it collapse into nonsense?
demo.closing: The demo must show that sequential generation keeps roads geometrically sane even when the input is noisy, whereas parallel generation (predicting all elements independently) produces broken maps.
